group.title: Arts and criticism
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The whole body of work produced by an artist or writer.
examples: This novel is the darkest in her entire {oeuvre}.
wrong: His oeuvre consists of only the one painting he never finished.

words.meaning: Built from a familiar pattern, with no surprises or originality.
examples: The plot is {formulaic}: meet, quarrel, split up, reunite.
wrong: The formulaic script broke every rule and surprised every viewer.

words.meaning: A work that imitates the style of another artist or period.
examples: The film is a playful {pastiche} of old detective movies.
wrong: The pastiche was completely original and copied no one.

words.meaning: Something made or done to show respect for an earlier artist or work.
examples: The opening scene is a {homage} to a classic silent film.
wrong: The director paid homage to the old master by mocking him.

words.meaning: A minor follower or imitator of an important artist or thinker.
examples: The great painter left behind a crowd of {epigones} who copied his style.
wrong: As an epigone, she invented a style that no one before her had tried.

words.meaning: Used so often that it has lost its effect.
examples: The script was full of {hackneyed} lines about true love.
wrong: His hackneyed phrase was something no one had ever heard.

words.meaning: Dull and unoriginal because it has been said too often.
examples: The ending offered a {trite} message about following your dreams.
wrong: Her trite insight surprised everyone with its freshness.

words.meaning: Ordinary and dull, lacking imagination.
examples: The acting was fine, but the direction was {pedestrian}.
wrong: The pedestrian staging dazzled critics with its daring ideas.

words.meaning: Competent and solid but not brilliant or inspired.
examples: It is a {workmanlike} thriller that does its job and no more.
wrong: The workmanlike performance was a dazzling stroke of genius.

words.meaning: Showing exceptional technical skill.
examples: Her {virtuosic} solo earned a standing ovation.
wrong: His virtuosic playing was full of clumsy wrong notes.

words.meaning: Showy, daring and done with great skill.
examples: The film opens with a {bravura} ten-minute single shot.
wrong: It was a bravura performance, timid and barely noticeable.

words.meaning: Made to please the artist rather than the audience, often too long or showy.
examples: The three-hour cut feels {self-indulgent} and badly needs editing.
wrong: Her tight, disciplined album is the least self-indulgent kind of work.

words.meaning: Works produced by an artist or writer when young.
examples: The exhibition includes the poet’s {juvenilia}, written at fourteen.
wrong: These juvenilia were the last poems he wrote in old age.

words.meaning: Accepted as one of the most important works in a field.
examples: The novel is now a {canonical} text taught in every school.
wrong: The canonical work is unknown and never studied.

words.meaning: A sudden, comic drop from a serious or grand tone to something silly.
examples: The tragic speech collapsed into {bathos} when the hero tripped over a cat.
wrong: The scene’s bathos lifted it steadily to ever greater dignity.

words.meaning: Appealing to the intellect rather than the emotions.
examples: It is a cool, {cerebral} film that rewards close attention.
wrong: The cerebral thriller relied only on gut feelings and cheap scares.

words.meaning: Too elaborate or emotional in style.
examples: The poem’s {overwrought} imagery buried its simple idea.
wrong: The overwrought prose was spare, calm and plain.

words.meaning: Having an artificial style that draws attention to itself.
examples: His later paintings became {mannered} and self-conscious.
wrong: Her mannered acting felt completely natural and effortless.

words.meaning: Too decorated and elaborate, especially in language.
examples: The speech was {florid}, full of grand phrases and little sense.
wrong: His florid writing used the plainest words possible.

words.meaning: Writing that is too elaborate and emotional.
examples: The editor cut pages of {purple prose} about sunsets.
wrong: The report was purple prose, dry and strictly factual.

words.meaning: Pompous, heavy and boring to read or listen to.
examples: The {turgid} essay took an hour to say almost nothing.
wrong: The turgid article was light, clear and quick to read.

words.meaning: A film director whose personal style marks everything they make.
examples: Fans can spot an {auteur}’s work from a single shot.
wrong: The auteur had no personal style and simply followed the studio’s orders.

words.meaning: Strongly attacking or defending an opinion.
examples: The documentary is openly {polemical}, not balanced.
wrong: His polemical essay carefully avoided taking any side.

words.meaning: To mock someone or something publicly with humor.
examples: The sketch show {lampooned} the prime minister every week.
wrong: The cartoonist lampooned the mayor by praising him solemnly.

words.meaning: The final part of a story, where everything is explained or resolved.
examples: The {denouement} reveals who wrote the anonymous letters.
wrong: The denouement comes on the first page and starts the mystery.

words.meaning: A theme, image or tune that keeps returning in a work.
examples: Water is a {leitmotif} running through all her novels.
wrong: The leitmotif appears only once and never returns.

words.meaning: A common theme or device used again and again in a genre.
examples: The chosen-one hero is a familiar {trope} of fantasy fiction.
wrong: The trope was something no writer had ever used before.

words.meaning: A hidden meaning beneath the obvious words or action.
examples: The {subtext} of the dinner scene is the couple’s failing marriage.
wrong: The subtext was stated openly in the very first line.

words.meaning: The strong contrast of light and dark in a picture.
examples: The painter used {chiaroscuro} to make the faces glow out of shadow.
wrong: The chiaroscuro was flat, with no light or shade at all.

words.meaning: The record of where an artwork came from and who has owned it.
examples: Experts traced the {provenance} of the vase back to 1820.
wrong: The provenance of the painting was the color of its frame.

words.meaning: Praise and approval.
examples: The young director won {plaudits} for her first feature.
wrong: The flop earned plaudits in the form of harsh reviews.

words.meaning: A speech or piece of writing full of high praise.
examples: The review was a glowing {encomium} to the young pianist.
wrong: His encomium savagely attacked every part of the book.

words.meaning: Too much sentimentality in music, film or writing.
examples: The final scene drowns in {schmaltz}, with violins and tearful hugs.
wrong: The cold, unsentimental film was full of schmaltz.

words.meaning: To criticize something by praising it only weakly.
examples: Calling the film ’perfectly adequate’ is to {damn it with faint praise}.
wrong: He damned the book with faint praise by calling it a timeless masterpiece.

words.meaning: A person with a refined love of art and beauty.
examples: An {aesthete} to the core, he filled his flat with rare prints.
wrong: As an aesthete, she cared nothing for art or beauty.

words.meaning: Someone who dabbles in an art or subject without serious study.
examples: He is a {dilettante} who paints a little and writes a little.
wrong: A dilettante, she spent forty years mastering one instrument.

words.meaning: A public speech or text that praises someone very highly.
examples: The biography reads less like history than a {panegyric}.
wrong: His panegyric listed every fault of the retiring director.

words.meaning: Easy to enjoy and moderately serious, without being demanding.
examples: The festival favors {middlebrow} dramas that please a wide audience.
wrong: The middlebrow novel was so difficult that only scholars read it.

words.meaning: Too sweet or sentimental.
examples: The film’s {saccharine} ending felt false after such a dark story.
wrong: The saccharine song was harsh, bitter and cold.

words.meaning: Attractive on the surface but having no real value.
examples: The show dazzles with {meretricious} special effects but no story.
wrong: The meretricious display had deep, lasting worth.
